turns.doctor_question: Hello, it’s nice to meet you. What brings you in today?
turns.patient_response: Hi. It's nice to meet you too. Um, I guess I came in because I've been having a really hard time lately with... well, with how I look. There's this spot, just around my nose and cheek, where it looks uneven to me. I see it every time I take a photo, and the fluorescent lights at the store where I work as a cashier just make it look so obvious. I keep getting stuck on it. My friends and family tell me they don't see anything wrong, but I just can't shake the feeling that it's the very first thing every customer and my manager notices when they look at me. It's just really starting to bother me.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient reports being persistently preoccupied with a perceived uneven spot on their nose and cheek that others say they cannot see, believing it is immediately noticeable to others.

turns.doctor_question: How certain are you that other people notice this uneven spot as much as you do?
turns.patient_response: Um, I guess I'm not entirely certain. I mean, my family and friends say they don't see it, and no customer has ever actually pointed it out or anything. But... when I'm standing there under those bright lights, I just feel like everyone is staring right at it. It's hard to believe they don't see it when it looks so obvious to me. So, I don't know for sure, but it definitely feels like they do.

turns.doctor_question: How often do you check or try to hide the uneven spot in mirrors, photos, or other reflections?
turns.patient_response: Well, pretty often, I guess. Especially at work. Like, on my breaks, I almost always end up going to the bathroom just to check my face in the mirror. I'll stand there and try fixing my hair around it to sort of cover the spot up. And... I also catch myself comparing my face to the girls who come through my checkout line. Sometimes I get so caught up checking the mirror and adjusting my hair that I actually take way too long, and I end up being late getting back to the register.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient reports frequently checking the mirror, adjusting their hair to cover the spot, and comparing their appearance to others, leading to occupational delay.

turns.doctor_question: Do you have any repetitive rituals or checking behaviors that are unrelated to your appearance?
turns.patient_response: Um, no, not really. I don't think so. I mean, I don't have any other habits like that. It's really just the stuff with my face and the mirror. I don't feel the need to check locks or wash my hands a certain number of times or anything like that, if that's what you mean. It's just... just my appearance that I get stuck on.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient confirms having repetitive behaviors focused on their appearance, specifically noting habits involving their face and the mirror.
symptom_reasoning.S066: The patient explicitly denies non-appearance-related compulsions, stating they do not have rituals like checking locks or compulsive hand washing.

turns.doctor_question: When you are in social situations, do you worry about being judged or embarrassed even when you are not thinking about your appearance?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. If I'm not thinking about my face, I'm usually fine around other people. I don't really worry about saying the wrong thing or, like, embarrassing myself in general. It's really just... the uneven spot. That's the only thing that makes me feel like people are judging me. If I could just fix that, I wouldn't worry about being around people at all.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient identifies an 'uneven spot' on their face as the central source of their distress and fear of judgment, confirming preoccupation with a perceived facial flaw.

turns.doctor_question: How long have you been preoccupied with the uneven spot on your face?
turns.patient_response: I'm not really sure exactly when it started, to be honest. I guess it's been a while, but I don't have a specific timeline or anything. It's just something I've been focused on for some time now.

turns.doctor_question: On a typical day, about how much time do you spend thinking about or checking the uneven spot?"
turns.patient_response: Um, it kind of adds up throughout the day. Like, when I'm at work—I work as a cashier—on my breaks I always end up checking my face in the bathroom mirror. I'll spend time fixing my hair around it, trying to hide it. And even when I'm working, I catch myself comparing myself to the girls who come through my checkout line. Sometimes I take so long looking in the mirror on my break that I'm actually late getting back to the register. So, I guess it's a pretty good chunk of time.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes engaging in repetitive mirror checking, camouflaging her hair to hide the flaw, and comparing herself to customers, to the point of being late back to work.
